quotes.t: I have fought sixty battles and I have learned nothing which I did not know at the beginning.
quotes.source: Gourgaud's Journal de Sainte-Hélène, entry 25 December 1817

quotes.t: I never was truly my own master but was always ruled by circumstances.
quotes.source: Mémorial de Sainte Hélène (Las Cases), conversation 11 November 1816

quotes.t: What I have done up to this is nothing. I am only at the beginning of the course I must run.
quotes.source: Memoirs of Count Miot de Melito (1881 trans.), Vol. II, p. 94

quotes.t: Impermanence becomes vivid in the present moment; so do compassion and wonder and courage. And so does fear.
Meditation is just gently coming back again and again to what's right here.
The main point is that we all need to be reminded and encouraged to relax with whatever arises and bring whatever we encounter to the path.
To see once is better than to hear a hundred times.
One joy shatters a hundred griefs.
Do not confine your children to your own learning, for they were born in another time.
Just study Buddhism. Don't follow the sentiments of the world.
When other sects speak well of Zen, the first thing that they praise is its poverty.
Body and mind will drop away of themselves, and your original face will manifest itself.
Nothing is so much to be feared as fear.
I am grateful for what I am and have. My thanksgiving is perpetual.
For many years I was self-appointed inspector of snowstorms and rainstorms, and did my duty faithfully, though I never received one cent for it.
Peace has been said to be indivisible; so is freedom, so is prosperity now, and so also is disaster in this One World that can no longer be split into isolated fragments.
Where freedom is menaced or justice threatened or where aggression takes place, we cannot be and shall not be neutral.
quotes.source: Address to the US Congress, 13 October 1949

quotes.t: The light has gone out, I said, and yet I was wrong. For the light that shone in this country was no ordinary light.
quotes.source: The Light Has Gone Out speech, 30 January 1948

quotes.t: No one should be discouraged, Theaetetus, who can make constant progress, even though it be slow.
All knowledge, when separated from justice and virtue, is seen to be cunning and not wisdom.
Knowledge is the food of the soul.
How I wish that wisdom could be infused by touch, out of the fuller into the emptier man, as water runs through wool out of a fuller cup into an emptier one.
How singular is the thing called pleasure, and how curiously related to pain, which might be thought to be the opposite of it.
Beloved Pan, and all ye other gods who haunt this place, give me beauty in the inward soul; and may the outward and inward man be at one.
All mortals are equal; it is not their birth, but virtue itself that makes the difference.
We all look for happiness, but without knowing where to find it: like drunkards who look for their house, knowing dimly that they have one.
To hold a pen is to be at war.
Now, what I want is, Facts. Teach these boys and girls nothing but Facts.
The civility which money will purchase, is rarely extended to those who have none.
quotes.source: Sketches by Boz, Our Parish, Chapter 5: The Broker's Man

quotes.t: What is the odds so long as the fire of soul is kindled at the taper of conviviality, and the wing of friendship never moults a feather!
We never know how high we are till we are called to rise.
To make a prairie it takes a clover and one bee.
My life closed twice before its close; it yet remains to see if Immortality unveil a third event to me.
What good shall I do this day?
Glass, china, and reputation are easily cracked, and never well mended.
Wealth is not his that has it, but his that enjoys it.
We must use time creatively, in the knowledge that the time is always ripe to do right.
Let us not seek to satisfy our thirst for freedom by drinking from the cup of bitterness and hatred.
We are not makers of history; we are made by history.
Why not seize the pleasure at once? How often is happiness destroyed by preparation, foolish preparation!
A woman especially, if she have the misfortune of knowing anything, should conceal it as well as she can.
Surprises are foolish things. The pleasure is not enhanced, and the inconvenience is often considerable.
To be too conscious is an illness — a real thorough-going illness.
Man grows used to everything, the scoundrel!
Life is paradise, and we are all in paradise, but we won't see it, if we would, we should have heaven on earth the next day.
We sometimes encounter people, even perfect strangers, who begin to interest us at first sight, somehow suddenly, all at once, before a word has been spoken.
I am a sick man. I am a spiteful man.
I did not bow down to you, I bowed down to all the suffering of humanity.
The only absolute knowledge attainable by man is that life is meaningless.
If there are as many minds as there are heads, then surely there must be as many kinds of love as there are hearts.
If we admit that human life can be ruled by reason, then all possibility of life is destroyed.

Anxiety is love's greatest killer. It creates the failures. It makes others feel as you might when a drowning man holds on to you. You want to save him, but you know he will strangle you with his panic.
quotes.source: The Diary of Anais Nin, Vol. 4 (1944-1947)

quotes.t: We travel, some of us forever, to seek other states, other lives, other souls.
quotes.source: The Diary of Anais Nin, Vol. 7 (1966-1974)

quotes.t: How wrong it is for woman to expect the man to build the world she wants, rather than set out to create it herself.
quotes.source: The Diary of Anais Nin, Vol. 5 (1947-1955)

quotes.t: You can be lonely even when you are loved by many people, since you are still not anybody's one and only.
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl

quotes.t: What is done cannot be undone, but one can prevent it happening again.
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl

quotes.t: Women should be respected as well! Generally speaking, men are held in great esteem in all parts of the world, so why shouldn't women have their share?
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl

quotes.t: Ubuntu is very difficult to render into a Western language. It speaks of the very essence of being human.
God's dream is that you and I and all of us will realize that we are family, that we are made for togetherness, for goodness, and for compassion.
We are made for loving. If we don't love, we will be like plants without water.
Learn to see in another's calamity the ills which you should avoid.
quotes.source: Sententiae, Maxim 120 (trans. Darius Lyman, The Moral Sayings of Publius Syrus, 1856)

quotes.t: The end of man is an action, and not a thought, though it were the noblest.
What is the meaning of life? That was all — a simple question; one that tended to close in on one with years.
quotes.source: To the Lighthouse, Part III, Chapter 3 (1927)

quotes.t: Nothing is more painful to the human mind than, after the feelings have been worked up by a quick succession of events, the dead calmness of inaction and certainty which follows and deprives the soul both of hope and fear.
quotes.source: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus, Volume II, Chapter 1 (1818)

quotes.t: Love is my religion — I could die for that.
Democracy is not merely a form of government. It is primarily a mode of associated living, of conjoint communicated experience.
In the space which thought creates around itself there is no love.
God will not look you over for medals, degrees or diplomas, but for scars.
quotes.source: Roycroft Dictionary and Book of Epigrams (1923), p. 122

quotes.t: When angry, count ten, before you speak; if very angry, an hundred.
quotes.source: Letter to Thomas Jefferson Smith, 21 February 1825 (A Decalogue of Canons for observation in practical life)

quotes.t: Your work is going to fill a large part of your life, and the only way to be truly satisfied is to do what you believe is great work.
It's an infernal nuisance to love Life as I do. I seem to love it more as time goes on rather than less. It never becomes a habit to me. It's always a marvel.
quotes.source: Letter to Anne Estelle Rice, 21 May 1921

quotes.t: Nothing is stronger than habit.
It is a pity that doing one's best does not always answer.
I have found that, to make a contented slave, it is necessary to make a thoughtless one.
quotes.source: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (1845)

quotes.t: Whatever satisfies the soul is truth.
Friendship is the only thing in the world concerning the usefulness of which all mankind are agreed.
Order is the shape upon which beauty depends.
Life isn't as serious as the mind makes it out to be.
quotes.source: A New Earth: Awakening to Your Life's Purpose (2005), Chapter 1

quotes.t: No one can live entirely on their own, nor can any country or society exist in isolation.
quotes.source: "Extreme Poverty: The Gravest Violation of Human Rights", The Japan Times, 14 December 2006

quotes.t: Anyone who says that the artist's sphere leaves no room for questions, but deals exclusively with answers, has never done any writing or done anything with imagery.
A goal properly set is halfway reached.
I know where I'm going and I know the truth, and I don't have to be what you want me to be. I'm free to be what I want.
quotes.source: Press conference, 27 February 1964 (as quoted in The New York Times)

quotes.t: Come, my friends, 'tis not too late to seek a newer world.
I never did a day's work in my life, it was all fun.
quotes.source: As quoted in Edison & Ford Quote Book (2003)

quotes.t: Success is nothing more than a few simple disciplines, practiced every day.

The only true voyage of discovery, the only fountain of Eternal Youth, would be not to visit strange lands but to possess other eyes, to behold the universe through the eyes of another, of a hundred others, to behold the hundred universes that each of them beholds, that each of them is.
quotes.source: The Captive (La Prisonnière, 1923), tr. C. K. Scott Moncrieff

quotes.t: We are born weak, we need strength; helpless, we need aid; foolish, we need reason. All that we lack at birth, all that we need when we come to man's estate, is the gift of education.
The sad truth of the matter is that most evil is done by people who never made up their minds to be or do either evil or good.
quotes.source: The Life of the Mind, Vol. 1: Thinking (1978)

quotes.t: Philosophy is written in that great book which ever lies before our eyes — I mean the universe — but we cannot understand it if we do not first learn the language and grasp the symbols, in which it is written.
quotes.source: The Assayer (Il Saggiatore, 1623), tr. Thomas Salusbury (1661)

quotes.t: The life so short, the craft so long to learn.
The truth may be stretched thin, but it never breaks, and it always surfaces above lies, as oil floats on water.
quotes.source: Don Quixote, Part II, ch. 10, tr. John Ormsby (1885)

quotes.t: For even as it is better to enlighten than merely to shine, so is it better to give to others the fruits of one's contemplation than merely to contemplate.
The mountains are calling and I must go, and I will work on while I can, studying incessantly.
quotes.source: Letter to Sarah Muir Galloway, 3 September 1873

quotes.t: It is the greatest happiness of the greatest number that is the measure of right and wrong.
People will not look forward to posterity, who never look backward to their ancestors.
quotes.source: Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790)

quotes.t: Where there is no common power, there is no law; where no law, no injustice.
Against stupidity the very gods themselves contend in vain.
quotes.source: The Maid of Orleans (Die Jungfrau von Orleans, 1801), Act III, sc. vi, tr. Anna Swanwick

quotes.t: I am looking for a man.
quotes.source: Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI, §41 (Diogenes Laërtius)

quotes.t: I would rather stand three times with a shield in battle than give birth once.
quotes.source: Medea (431 BC), lines 248–251, tr. David Kovacs (1994)

quotes.t: Some men say an army of horse and some men say an army on foot and some men say an army of ships is the most beautiful thing on the black earth. But I say it is what you love.
quotes.source: Fragment 16, tr. Anne Carson (If Not, Winter, 2002)

Alfred Tennyson.bio: English Poet Laureate; author of In Memoriam and Ulysses.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Anne Frank.bio: German-born Jewish diarist whose diary documents life in hiding during the Holocaust.

Anton Chekhov.bio: Anton Chekhov was a Russian playwright and master of the short story, a practising doctor who wrote The Cherry Orchard, Uncle Vanya and hundreds of stories. His restrained, humane art reshaped both the theatre and short fiction of the 20th century.

B.R. Ambedkar.bio: Indian jurist and social reformer who chaired the drafting of India's Constitution and campaigned against caste discrimination.

Benjamin Franklin.bio: American polymath - printer, scientist, diplomat - and a Founding Father of the United States.

Charles Dickens.bio: English novelist and social critic; author of A Christmas Carol, Oliver Twist and Great Expectations.

Charlotte Brontë.bio: English novelist, author of Jane Eyre.
Charlotte Brontë.credit: Alonzo Chappel, Public domain (File: File:Charlotte Bronte by Alonzo Chappel.jpg)

Cicero.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman, lawyer and orator considered the master of Latin prose. His speeches, letters and philosophical works, including On Friendship, transmitted Greek philosophy to the Roman world.

Daisaku Ikeda.bio: Daisaku Ikeda was a Japanese Buddhist philosopher, educator and peace activist who led the Soka Gakkai lay Buddhist movement and founded Soka University. He wrote extensively on Buddhism, dialogue and peace.

Desmond Tutu.bio: South African Anglican archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1984) who campaigned against apartheid.

Diogenes.bio: Greek philosopher (c. 412–323 BCE), one of the founders of Cynicism.

Dogen.bio: Founder of the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan and author of the Shōbōgenzō, a landmark of Buddhist philosophy.

Eckhart Tolle.bio: Eckhart Tolle is a German-born spiritual teacher living in Canada, author of The Power of Now (1997) and A New Earth (2005), books on presence and the ego that became international bestsellers.

Edmund Burke.bio: Edmund Burke was an Irish-born British statesman and political thinker, celebrated as a parliamentary orator. His Reflections on the Revolution in France made him a founding voice of modern conservatism, while he also supported American grievances and prosecuted abuses in India.

Elbert Hubbard.bio: Elbert Hubbard was an American writer, publisher and philosopher who founded the Roycroft arts-and-crafts community. His essay "A Message to Garcia" (1899) was one of the most widely reprinted works of its era; he died in the sinking of the Lusitania.

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Euripides.bio: Euripides was an Athenian tragedian, one of the three great playwrights of classical Greek theatre alongside Aeschylus and Sophocles. His plays, including Medea and The Bacchae, explored psychology and questioned traditional myths.

Frederick Douglass.bio: American abolitionist and writer who escaped slavery and became a leading voice against it.

Friedrich Schiller.bio: German poet, philosopher, historian and playwright; author of the Wallenstein trilogy, Don Carlos and the 'Ode to Joy'.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.bio: Russian novelist, author of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.

Galileo Galilei.bio: Galileo Galilei was an Italian astronomer and physicist whose telescopic observations supported the heliocentric model of the solar system. His defence of Copernican astronomy brought him into conflict with the Catholic Church.

Geoffrey Chaucer.bio: English poet, author of The Canterbury Tales; often called the father of English literature.

Hannah Arendt.bio: Hannah Arendt was a German-American political theorist whose works include The Origins of Totalitarianism and The Human Condition. She coined the phrase 'the banality of evil' in her report on the Eichmann trial.

Henry David Thoreau.bio: American writer known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jawaharlal Nehru.bio: Leader of India's independence movement and the country's first Prime Minister (1947-1964).

Jean-Jacques Rousseau.bio: Genevan philosopher whose Social Contract shaped modern political thought.

Jeremy Bentham.bio: English philosopher and founder of utilitarianism.

Jiddu Krishnamurti.bio: Indian philosopher and speaker on the nature of mind, meditation, and human freedom; rejected all guru roles.

Jim Rohn.bio: Emanuel James Rohn, known as Jim Rohn, was an American entrepreneur and motivational speaker whose seminars and books on personal development influenced a generation of speakers, including Tony Robbins.

John Keats.bio: English Romantic poet of the great Odes, including Ode to a Nightingale.

John Muir.bio: John Muir was a Scottish-American naturalist, author and early advocate for the preservation of wilderness in the United States. He co-founded the Sierra Club, and his writings helped inspire the creation of national parks including Yosemite.

Katherine Mansfield.bio: New Zealand modernist short-story writer, a leading figure of early 20th-century literature alongside Joyce and Woolf.
Katherine Mansfield.credit: Archives New Zealand from New Zealand, CC BY-SA 2.0

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Marcel Proust.bio: Marcel Proust was a French novelist whose seven-volume 'In Search of Lost Time' ('À la recherche du temps perdu'), published between 1913 and 1927, is regarded as one of the greatest works of modern literature, exploring memory, time and art.

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Mary Shelley.bio: English novelist, author of Frankenstein, a founding work of science fiction.

Miguel de Cervantes.bio: Spanish novelist, poet and playwright best known for Don Quixote.

Muhammad Ali.bio: American heavyweight boxing champion and cultural icon known as much for his activism as his titles.

Napoleon Bonaparte.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French in 1804. His Napoleonic Wars reshaped Europe, and his Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems worldwide. He died in exile on Saint Helena.

Ovid.bio: Ovid was a Roman poet celebrated for the Metamorphoses, a vast narrative poem of mythological transformations. Exiled by the emperor Augustus to the Black Sea coast, he spent his last decade writing poems of lament and endurance.

Pearl Buck.bio: Pearl S. Buck was an American writer who spent much of her early life in China, where her parents were missionaries. Her novel The Good Earth won the Pulitzer Prize, and she received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938.

Pema Chodron.bio: Pema Chodron is an American nun in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and a widely read author and teacher. Her books, including When Things Fall Apart, bring Buddhist teachings on compassion and difficulty to a broad audience.

Plato.bio: Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and author of The Republic.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

Sappho.bio: Greek lyric poet (c. 630 – c. 570 BCE) from the island of Lesbos, one of the great lyric poets of antiquity.

Socrates.bio: Greek philosopher of Athens, central figure of Western philosophy; left no writings.

Steve Jobs.bio: Co-founder of Apple, Steve Jobs helped launch the personal computer era and later reinvented music, phones and tablets with the iPod, iPhone and iPad. Forced out of Apple in 1985, he founded NeXT and built Pixar into a major studio before returning in 1997 to rescue the company he had started.

Thomas Aquinas.bio: Thomas Aquinas was an Italian Dominican friar and the foremost scholastic theologian of the Middle Ages. His Summa Theologica attempted a complete rational account of Christian doctrine and remains central to Catholic philosophy.

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Thomas Edison.bio: Thomas Edison was an American inventor who developed the phonograph, the motion picture camera and the first practical electric light bulb. He held over a thousand US patents and founded the first industrial research laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey.

Thomas Jefferson.bio: Thomas Jefferson was an American statesman and Founding Father who wrote the Declaration of Independence and served as the third President of the United States (1801–1809). He founded the University of Virginia and doubled the nation's size with the Louisiana Purchase.

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was a French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and historian famous for the novella Candide and for his witty defence of civil liberties, including freedom of speech and religion. He was one of the most prolific and influential writers of his age.

Walt Whitman.bio: American poet best known for the collection Leaves of Grass (1855).

Zig Ziglar.bio: Zig Ziglar was an American author and motivational speaker who became one of the most influential sales and personal-development trainers of the twentieth century. His book See You at the Top and his famous line 'Your attitude, not your aptitude, will determine your altitude' reached millions.
